Pangolins

By: Graham Coetzer | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The Pangolin is the most trafficked animal in the world, and South Africa is one of the hotspots for smugglers.

Unique Selling Point:
We have a source who is in contact with a wildlife smuggling syndicate. Amongst other things the syndicate has access to Pangolins and regularly sells them on the black market, where a live animal can fetch up to R150 000. The source is willing to setup a sting with us, in which we will setup a "buy" with members of the syndicate, capture everything on hidden camera, and then have the relevant law enforcement arrest the sellers and one of the main players in they syndicate, as well as have the Pangolins removed and rehabilitated.

Summary:
Of the 8 species of Pangolin found throughout Africa and Asia, 2 are critically endangered, 2 are endangered and 4 species are listed as threatened. Traditional Asian medicine believes the scales are a cure for a whole host of medical conditions including cancer. The scales are actually keratin, the same stuff our nails and hair consist of, and hold no medicinal value. Some Chinese operations claim their product comes from farming, but this is also false and all Pangolin products found in Asia are as a result of the huge smuggling operations both their and in Africa.

Further information:
Our insert will highlight the plight of the Pangolin in SA - an animal very few people have even heard of since our focus has traditionally been Rhino, Lion etc. The success of the story will be our sting, where we will need a presenter and the help of law enforcement. The last time we were in contact with the syndicate they had four Pangolins available in the Nelspruit / Pongola /Swaziland border areas. The risk for us is do we get the bust. I have had Sinethemba listen to a conversation which took place with the head of the syndicate and our source (in Zulu) and he says it all sounds legit. The source has been reliable in the past and has a vast amount of experience with wildlife in Africa. I will need extra budget items as listed below to go do the sting:

Extra Budget Items:
Travel (by car) to Nelspruit region, accommodation for presenter, source, cameraman and producer for 1 night (4 people).
Budget: Travel 1200km - R1000. Accom x 4 @R750 per person - R3000. S&T x 4 people x 2 days - R1440.
Total budget RR5440.

I am also happy if CAP prefers car rental and accommodation through Red Carpet. (Not sure where Accom will be because not sure where sting will take place)

Press Release:


Saving Pangolins
It’s a cute, nocturnal and scaly creature, but few people will ever see one. The pangolin is the most
trafficked mammal in the world, fetching up to R150 000 each on the black market. Across Africa, over a
million have been removed from the wild over the last decade and South Africa is at the centre of the illegal
trade. Carte Blanche goes undercover to infiltrate a dangerous syndicate of smugglers and stop them in
their tracks.

Script:


Link Claire
It may come as a surprise to most people that the most trafficked mammal in the world is not the rhino or the lion or any of the big five, but it is a small scaled creature called the Pangolin.
Voice
Pangolins, or scaly anteaters, are poached for their scales, which are highly sought after in Asia where they are used in traditional medicine. We wanted to see how bad things were on the ground in South Africa, and started an undercover investigation. This week, we had a breakthrough as an insider let us know that two Pangolins were for sale in Limpopo by a poaching syndicate.
Sound Up Claire
We are on our way to Phalaborwa with our informant, who has set up a deal with a trafficker. The trafficker says that she knows of two Pangolins that are available for sale, but before we get the police to bust them we have to go inside and see if the Pangolins actually exist and if they’re alive.
Voice
Just outside of town our insider, who has asked not to appear on camera, received a call from the seller, known only as Leah.
Sound Up Claire
We’ve just arrived in Lulekane, which is near Phalaborwa, and we’re about to meet our trafficker. She says the house where the Pangolins are being kept is nearby.


Voice
What followed was one wild goose chase after another, as Leah directed us to several locations in Lulekane, only for our undercover team to find nothing when they arrived. It was obvious spotters along the route were checking our vehicle and it’s occupants. And then finally, after we threatened to pull out of the deal, Leah met us along the road and got into our vehicle.
Sound Up Hiddencam
Man: Mama, the money, must they bring R200 000 straight?
Woman: Ja.
Man: Ok.
Woman: When they bring the other one we pay them and take it. Your two…
Man: Let’s carry on with the two available.
Woman: Ja.
Voice
We were told we’d be taken to this house where we were not allowed to speak to anyone, use our phones or take any pictures. On arrival we were shown the luckless animals who were being kept in this shed.
Sound Up Hiddencam
Investigator: It’s alive?
Woman: This one? Mmmm
Investigator: And there’s only two?
Woman: Yes.
Voice
Our producer and camera man hightailed it back to the local police station under the pretence of going to fetch the cash, where members of the Limpopo Endangered Species Unit and a specialised anti poaching team called Hemmersbach Rhino Force were waiting.
Sound Up Claire
We’re following the police and the specialised anti poaching unit to bust the house and rescue the pangolins.
Voice
As the task force entered the premises, members of the syndicate made a run for it and all hell broke loose.

Sound Up Gunshots

Voice
The highly trained team used warning shots to subdue the syndicate, and they soon found themselves in custody. Thanks to the professional conduct of everyone involved, no one had been injured.

Sound Up Claire
So this is where they were holding the Pangolin for almost a week. We were surprised that they were still alive because they do not survive in captivity. They were going to be sold for a hundred thousand rand each. The assailants are behind us right now and we are trying to get more information about who the owner is and where they got them.
Voice
In total five men and Leah were arrested and charged with possession of endangered species. We followed SAPS as they took the Pangolins to a wildlife vet for a check up, where Dr Liesel Steinmann examined both of them.
Sound Up Liesel
Claire: Just on your first impression, how are they doing?
Liesel: They are looking ok, I think it helped that they were two together, and they are in a good condition at this stage, they appear healthy there’s no wounds, there’s no limping, they are walking well. So we’ll just assess them and then get them released back into the wild as soon as possible.


Voice
Assisting Liesel was Hemmersbach Rhino Force member Glen Thompson. An important part of the process is taking samples from the Pangolin scales to use in a national forensic database. Each sample is meticulously bagged and tagged to preserve the chain of custody.
Sound Up Glen
So I take a sample of the scales and from that they will be able to build up a DNA profile for that Pangolin. So one will be kept in the database and one will be used for court proceedings.
Link Claire
The samples that were collected from the Pangolins we rescued will come here, to the biobank at the national zoological gardens in pretoria.
Sound Up Prof Ray Jansen
So it’s a public facility, it’s a non profit facility, but it’s also a facility that’s officially recognised as a South African Police Service place where we do forensic analysis, we do DNA reports, chain of custody sampling of endangered species such as Pangolins, Rhinos, and this facility provides those official reports which are then used in court cases.
Voice
Professor Ray Jansen is the Chairman of the African Pangolin Working Group and a self proclaimed Pangolin fanatic. He says as Asian Pangolins have been hunted to near extinction, demand has grown for the African species.
Sound Up Ray
The Asian demand for African Pangolins has quadrupled in the last few years. This year alone we’ve intercepted 34.7 tonnes of African Pangolin scales that have left Africa’s shores, thats anything between 30 and 60 thousand Pangolins.
Voice
Nicci Wright is a wildlife rehabilitation specialist at the Johannesburg Wildlife Veterinary Hospital and a member of the Humane Society International. She plays a key role in the Working Group, rehabilitating Pangolins removed from the illicit trade.
Sound Up Nicci
It really has been getting worse and worse. There are more and more coming off the trade all throughout Southern Africa including South Africa.
Voice
Wright has developed a specialised rehabilitation process for the animals, which includes keeping them sedated for the first 24 hours to stabilise them.
Sound Up Nicci
And then after that we start walking them and take them out to forage. Because as I say they don’t eat in captivity.
Voice
Once the Pangolin is fully rehabilitated, Wright releases them into their natural habitat and the animals are monitored via telemetry trackers. Back at the bio bank Professor Desiré Dalton and her team can identify poaching hotspots by forensically examining the DNA from scale samples they receive.
Sound Up Desire Dalton
So we can look at that and tell what species it is, and then we can also look at the nuclear DNA to find the geographic locality of the animal.
Voice
Pangolin scales consist mostly of Keratin, the same substance our hair and nails are made of. It has absolutely no medicinal value, but Professor Jansen says a lack of awareness and a belief system dating back thousands of years are not going to change overnight.
Sound Up Ray
This is exactly what they want. So they grind up these scales into powder, and I’ve identified 60 different Chinese remedies that use ground Pangolin powdered scales. So it’s a remedy it’s an ingredient in these Chinese medicines. And if you think of how large the population now is and they’ve been doing this for 5 to 10 thousand years it’s an incredibly difficult thing to stop.
Voice
Pangolins are also available as bushmeat in many parts of Africa, where the animals are sold along with a whole variety of species not normally seen on western menu’s. From the 1st of January this year CITES appendix 1 allows no form of commercial trade in Pangolins, but we found them being sold in the Johannesburg CBD at the Mai-Mai muthi market.
Sound Up Hiddencam
Investigator: What is that?
Man: Pangolin
Investigator: What do you use it for?
Man: Ja for me, for protection.
Voice
Many people believe Pangolin scales offer protection from evil influences. Professor Jansen says though illegal, the local trade is not a major concern.
Sound Up Prof Ray Jansen
The demand is actually very little, and it actually can be sustainable. Its regarded in traditional medicine in South Africa as a very important species. So they don’t want to lose the species out of the culture so they use very little of it. So that’s almost sustainable.
Voice
In the wild, Pangolin’s have few natural predators, as their very hard scales provide protection against most attackers. But when it comes to humans, the Pangolins greatest protection is also it’s worst enemy.
Sound Up Glen Thompson
If it is startled in the bush it rolls up into a little ball, you just pick up and walk off. It won’t try defend itself or anything like that. That is why it’s so easy to get them.
Voice
The two Pangolins we rescued, who we’ve dubbed Abbot and Costello, were released on thursday at a secret and relatively safe location with a clean bill of health. According to Glen they marched off happily into the sunset. The members of the syndicate who were arrested will be applying for bail on the 16th of this month, and until then remain in custody. If Pangolins aren’t protected, poaching operations in South Africa and around the continent will continue to increase, and they might end up as just another statistic.
